Measured on this build: the shade does NOT follow the vote. It stays at 120. The call is accepted, but the panel takes its mode from the foreground app\'s window, and SystemUI\'s shade, quick settings and lock screen are system overlays with no activity in that stack — so nothing ever reads the override.\n\nThe switch is kept for builds that behave differently. Where such a vote does land it pins the display rather than one app, and holds the lock screen and always-on display there too. Arm all always skips this row.
A rootless per-app refresh-rate unlock for the OnePlus 15 on OxygenOS 16. Here is what it actually does to your phone.

Pins the refresh rate — 60, 90, 120, 144 or 165 Hz — on the apps you pick. Choose the rate at the top, then tap an app to arm it at that rate; tap the row\'s details for a rate that app alone should use. Arm all sweeps the whole list, Re-arm re-sends the saved set, Clear withdraws everything. The armed set survives reboots.

OxygenOS carries a display service, oplusscreenmode, whose requestGameRefreshRate call has no permission check on the caller — so any app can ask for a rate on behalf of any package. It is the same request the system\'s own game mode uses, which is why no root is needed and why nothing is patched or replaced. The vendor\'s rate ids are not in Hz order (90 comes before 60), which is what an early build had swapped.
The vote is a pin, not a ceiling

The request sets the panel\'s minimum and maximum to the same rate, so while an armed app is on screen the panel has no range to move inside. Each rate selects a panel mode with its own idle floor, measured on this build: 165 rests at 55 Hz, 144 near 48, 60 and 90 at 30, and 120 goes all the way down to 1.

Game engines re-pin their own frame rate whenever they take focus, which overwrites a one-shot request. The watchdog is a quiet foreground service that re-issues the vote while the screen is on, so ours lands after theirs and wins. Its notification says how many apps it is holding; with nothing armed it stops itself.
Why the app on screen matters

The system writes the request onto the windows of the package it names, and the panel follows whichever write landed last. So every sweep ends on the app you are actually using — one that ended on a background app would hand the display a vote for windows that do not exist and drop the pin it had just set, which is what arming hundreds of apps used to do to itself. Usage access (Settings, Foreground detection) is what lets the watchdog know which app that is; without it, only games the vendor\'s game daemon tracks can be recognised.

A held 165 vote cannot idle below 55 Hz, so a still screen keeps paying for frames nobody sees. When nothing on screen is moving, the watchdog swaps the vote for 120 — the one rate whose panel mode spans 1 to 120 — and the panel ramps down to 1 Hz while the vote itself stays held. Content that demands more than 120 gets the armed rate back in about 55 ms. Only 144 and 165 park: 120 already is the park, and 60 or 90 are ceilings you chose to keep faster content off the panel.
Arming the system UI or this app

The notification shade, quick settings and lock screen are drawn by SystemUI rather than by the app you are in, so they keep their own rate — 120, and arming SystemUI does not change that on this build. The vote is accepted and has no effect: the panel takes its mode from the foreground app\'s window, and SystemUI\'s are system overlays that never consult it. The row is kept for builds that behave differently, and Arm all always skips it, because where such a vote does land it pins the display rather than one app.\n\nThis app\'s own row does work, and doubles as a self-test: if 165 Armer\'s own screen reaches the rate you armed it at, votes are landing — and if it will not, nothing else will either.

Disarm withdraws the vote by asking for rate id 0, the vendor\'s own cancel — sending the rate again would only write the same pin back, which is why an older build could not disarm without a reboot. If an app ever stays pinned, that build refused the withdraw; a reboot always clears every vote, because the vendor keeps them in memory only.

The permanent per-app override the Settings app uses is permission-protected and closed to a rootless app, so a vote applies only while its app is in the foreground. Video can judder when it is forced above its own cadence — pin those at 60 or leave them unarmed. Battery and heat rise with the rate and with the number of armed apps. An OTA can close the hole at any time, and a SecurityException in the log is what that looks like.

Settings has a Live log page. Arm165 lines are this app: vote results, screen: which app it sees in front of you, parked at 120 when it hands the panel over to the idle ramp, and parked hold: what the panel settled on. RefreshRate lines are the vendor framework\'s own rate changes. Share sends the buffer, which is the useful thing to attach to a bug report.
